extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional law, and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing normative principles about judicial review, impeachment, federalism, and the balance of powers in the United States as discussed in a political-theory/textbook chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial obedience to the Constitution over statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the United States the constitution governs the legislator as much as the private citizen; as it is the first of laws it cannot be modified by a law, and it is therefore just that the tribunals should obey the constitution in preference to any law.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative principle that the constitution is supreme and that judges are justified in applying the Constitution in preference to conflicting statutes. The text contrasts this with English practice and notes this condition is essential to the power of the judicature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power to refuse to apply unconstitutional laws (judicial review) and its political effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whenever a law which the judge holds to be unconstitutional is argued in a tribunal of the United States he may refuse to admit it as a rule; this power ... gives rise to immense political influence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that a judge's refusal to apply a statute diminishes the law's moral cogency, encourages avoidance, multiplies similar suits, and ultimately forces constitutional amendment or legislative repeal. Emphasizes the long-term political consequences of case-by-case judicial invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit judicial review to disputes tied to private interests (case-specific litigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: By connecting the censorship of the laws with the private interests of members of the community, and by intimately uniting the prosecution of the law with the prosecution of an individual, legislation is protected from wanton assailants and from the daily aggressions of party spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates that judicial review operate through ordinary lawsuits brought by parties with concrete interests, not through abstract or theoretical attacks by judges. This linkage conceals political importance, restricts publicity of attacks, and reduces partisan misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid broad/theoretical judicial attacks on legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the judge had been empowered to contest the laws on the ground of theoretical generalities, if he had been enabled to open an attack or to pass a censure on the legislator, he would have played a prominent part in the political sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies an anti-pattern: judges issuing abstract censures would politicize the judiciary and risk aligning judges as champions or antagonists of parties. Recommends keeping judicial determinations tied to concrete cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens' right to prosecute public officers in ordinary tribunals as a safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is perfectly natural that in a free country like America all the citizens should have the right of indicting public functionaries before the ordinary tribunals ... the right of minor prosecutions, which are within the reach of the whole community, is a better pledge of freedom than those great judicial actions which are rarely employed until it is too late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports decentralised, accessible legal accountability (minor prosecutions) rather than rare, exceptional processes (e.g., only impeachment). Notes that lawsuits are costly and thus require serious grounds, which tempers frivolous political litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer certainty and mildness of justice over harsh exceptional punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: When justice is more certain and more mild, it is at the same time more efficacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues historically that inflicting milder but certain penalties is more effective at reducing crime and tyranny than rare extreme punishments; used to justify ordinary-court accountability rather than extraordinary political punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens should not need sovereign/administrative permission to seek redress
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Art. 75 (Constitution de l’An VIII): the citizen who has been injured by the order of the sovereign is obliged to solicit from the sovereign permission to obtain redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condemns systems (illustrated by Conseil d’Etat practice) where administrative or executive organs can block prosecutions of public officers; recommends ordinary judicial access without needing permission from the sovereign or administrative council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment structure: legislative indictment and political judgment limited to public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States ... the House of Representatives arraigns the offender, and the Senate awards his sentence. ... those persons must belong to the class of public functionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the procedural design that one legislative chamber impeaches and the other tries, and that impeachment jurisdiction in the US is limited to public officers (unlike broader political tribunals in Europe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish administrative removal from criminal punishment (political jurisdiction limited in penalties)
rubrics_metrics.description: In America, when [political tribunals] have deprived the offender of his official rank, and have declared him incapable of filling any political office for the future, their jurisdiction terminates and that of the ordinary tribunals begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that political/judicial-political proceedings (e.g., impeachment) are principally administrative (removal/disqualification) while criminal penalties (liberty, life) require ordinary criminal trial and jury. Emphasizes separation of administrative sanction and criminal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction designed as a preventive/administrative measure (danger of broad latitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main object of the political jurisdiction ... is to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority which he has used amiss ... A political condemnation in the United States may, therefore, be looked upon as a preventive measure; and there is no reason for restricting the judges to the exact definitions of criminal law. Nothing can be more alarming than the excessive latitude with which political offences are described in the laws of America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that because removal/disqualification is easier than criminal punishment, political jurisdiction can be used more readily and thereby become a pervasive instrument of majority power. Recommends caution about vaguely worded offenses (e.g., 'maladministration') that permit broad political use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating prosecutorial and adjudicative bodies to reduce partisan vindictiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to be observed, in the first place, that in the United States the tribunal which passes sentence is composed of the same elements, and subject to the same influences, as the body which impeaches the offender, and that this uniformity gives an almost irresistible impulse to the vindictive passions of parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies institutional design risk: when the same political majority both impeaches and tries, partisan vengeance is more likely. Implies need for institutional checks or separation to mitigate party-driven convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require clear, limited grounds for impeachment rather than unlimited responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Article II., Section 4 ... 'removed from office on impeachment for, and conviction of, treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.' Many of the Constitutions of the States are even less explicit. ... in some constitutions no offences are specified, in order to subject the public functionaries to an unlimited responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates specification of impeachable offenses to avoid vague or limitless grounds (e.g., 'maladministration') that expand majority power to remove officials for routine political reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated federal powers with residual state sovereignty (federal exception, state rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Division of authority between the Federal Government and the States—The Government of the States is the rule, the Federal Government the exception. ... the attributes of the Federal Government were therefore carefully enumerated and all that was not included amongst them was declared to constitute a part of the privileges of the several Governments of the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of enumerated powers: the federal government is granted specific national competencies; all other powers remain with states. Text gives examples (bankruptcy, patents, commerce) and explains this arrangement reduces conflict and preserves state autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a high federal court to maintain the balance of power
rubrics_metrics.description: A high Federal court was created ... which was destined, amongst other functions, to maintain the balance of power which had been established by the Constitution between the two rival Governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation that a supreme/federal tribunal interpret the Constitution and resolve disputes between states and the union to preserve the intended federal-state balance. Notes the court's action is often indirect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal prerogatives: exclusive national functions (war, treaties, commerce, monetary system, post office, roads, bankruptcy, patents, taxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive right of making peace and war, of concluding treaties of commerce, of raising armies, and equipping fleets, was granted to the Union. ... The Union was invested with the power of controlling the monetary system, of directing the post office, and of opening the great roads ... Congress has the right of making a general law on bankruptcy ... to grant patents ... the Federal Government was endowed with an unlimited power of levying taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists concrete domains properly centralized in the federal government to serve national interests and ensure ability to fulfil obligations. Citations to constitutional sections and The Federalist are provided as support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit ex post facto laws and titles of nobility at state level
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus, whilst the power of modifying and changing their legislation at pleasure was preserved in all the republics, they were forbidden to enact ex post facto laws, or to create a class of nobles in their community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional constraints on state legislation: states retain legislative freedom but are restricted from retroactive criminalization and establishing hereditary/noble classes, preserving basic rights and equality under the union.
